en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The True Dhamma is indeed preserved in the Pali language alone; thus, this is the Illumination of the Human Eye.
And by means of the chosen protection;
that virtue which is well protected,
the beautiful Dhamma is protected.
It should be understood that right exertion is the root of all attainments.
"Monks, the undertaking of energy... [is so stated].
"It leads to great benefit.
Therefore, energy alone must be exerted;
for one who possesses energy, even the inconceivable comes to pass.
Just as a carpenter’s measuring line is the standard for them,
so too is this one for the wise.
Your prosperity is easy to recognize,
while your downfall is difficult to recognize;
you are one who desires the Dhamma.
"Dhammadessī parābhavo" means this is the nature (dhammatā),
that is, this is the inherent character (sabhāva);
it is said to be the fixed order (niyāma).
Of those phenomena that arise from a cause,
the Tathāgata has declared their cause.
I pay homage to the Three Jewels, which are ever-present.
I always pay homage to my teacher:
"May all things be auspicious for me in every way.
— *Naradakkhadīpanī*
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One;
salutation to the Lamp of Human Vision.
Homage to the one with all-seeing eyes;
to him who is completely liberated from saṃsāra,
to him who is completely liberated from saṃsāra.
The most excellent protection for the True Dharma and the Sangha,
by those who have attained mastery.
The Supreme Buddha, who has protected the perfection of virtue,
may he protect this work of composition.
May you be well-versed in the scriptures, wise,
and firmly established in moral discipline.
One devoted to mental tranquility,
even if he stands upon one's head—
thus it is said by the Supplicant.
Having paid homage to the Dhamma and the Saṅgha,
the leaders of the entire world,
[this was] requested by the Elder Tikakrapa.
And by the wise Māṇava,
this has been clearly and concisely set forth,
well-composed from various treatises.
I shall write this "Skill in Man";
let my wise ones behold it.
Having seen laziness as a source of fear,
Energy too brings security;
be those who have aroused energy—
this is the instruction of the Buddhas.
“Monks, the noble disciple who possesses energy abandons what is unwholesome and develops what is wholesome;
he abandons what is blameworthy and develops what is blameless.”
"He preserves himself in purity.
For one possessed of energy, what task indeed does not succeed?
Truly, personal effort never goes to waste.
"I know that one establishes [them] in happiness.
Just as a clod of earth thrown into the sky will certainly fall to the ground;"
In the same way, the word of the supreme Buddhas is constant and eternal;
the Buddhas are speakers of non-dual truth.
The Victors possess unfailing speech.
One who listens gains wisdom;
one who exerts himself finds wealth.
Therefore, holding the Pāḷi in high esteem,
behold this beautiful [text]:
it is characterized by obedience, learning, and wisdom.
What has been heard increases wisdom;
through wisdom one understands the meaning,
and the understood meaning brings happiness.
Constant meditation, debate,
observation of the systems of others,
and service to all branches of learning.
The quality that produces intelligence is this:
for one who is overly burdened by grief,
lazy, and lacking in vigor, [wisdom does not arise].
Therefore, having exerted effort,
let the virtuous seek true knowledge;
for even a superior person must first master a craft.
One should acquire wealth from others,
seek out counsel therefrom,
and speak words of truth.
First, one should not lose one's craft;
second, one should not lose one's wealth;
third, one should not lose one's wealth.
What will the fourth meaning accomplish?
They shine like unfading flowers worn as an ornament.
Thus do young men shine when they are training in their youth.
Therefore, indeed, [one should seek] that which is the repository of virtues.
A wise person, desiring their own welfare,
should train in that which is the supreme increase of wisdom.
One who desires their own welfare should not strive too much in a craft;
they should recognize what has been accomplished through knowledge and the like.
May the wind not blow upon you.
Study the true knowledge, practice virtue,
and dwell together with the wise.
One should perform work for the accumulation of wealth,
speak pleasant words,
and never indeed sleep.
The night garlanded with stars is for those who know to be kept awake.
Arise, sit up!
What is the use of your sleeping?
It is indeed good to call upon the knowledge of one's craft.
Train yourselves in true knowledge and tranquility.
O sons, always exert yourselves to seek out those who are deeply learned.
Because in the world those possessed of craft are renowned in all directions,
[so too was] the Sakyan form that existed in the city.
"I did not train in a craft; for one without a craft,
living is difficult"—
thus one regrets later.
Desiring to seek the welfare of the world and its activities,
one must always possess energy.
One should contemplate meaningful counsel.
In this world, one who possesses wealth and virtue becomes renowned in every direction.
The mortal who is virtuous and wise is honored by all the world;
he lives with true glory whose fame is widespread.
Fame is what truly lives for one;
for one devoid of fame and renown,
even though living, they are like the dead.
Faith is the supreme wealth of a person here;
the Dhamma well-practiced brings happiness;
truth indeed is the sweetest of tastes.
They say that the life lived by wisdom is the best.
For one who possesses mindfulness, there is always good fortune;
the mindful person thrives in happiness.
For one who possesses mindfulness, tomorrow is better;
they are liberated from enmity.
Do not let this opportunity slip away from you.
For those who have let the moment pass must grieve; therefore,
you should strive for the true goal,
as the moment has been granted to you.
Just as one who lacks skill at the oars does not reach his desired destination on the ocean,
so too it is here with one devoid of energy.
Therefore, one should undertake the teaching;
a person should indeed exert themselves until the goal is accomplished.
There is no purpose more beautiful than one accomplished;
there is nothing superior to patience.
Even with equal application of knowledge, [patience excels].
It brings happiness and is most auspicious;
for indeed, when both are present in abundance,
there is a perfect attainment through this twofold means.
Bodily deeds are accomplished,
as are verbal deeds and energy;
for tasks are not fulfilled by mere thoughts.
One should exert effort here;
one should act in anticipation,
knowing that to be for one's own welfare.
A wise person should not exert effort with the mindset of a cart-driver; rather,
he should proceed with his own work steadily.
The fruit indeed increases for one who is diligent;
but for one who is unstable and lazy,
there is neither the performance of the task nor its fruit.
A wise person should indeed aspire; he should not become despondent.
For I see myself as...
It happened exactly as he wished.
He became free from debt to his kinsmen,
and to the gods and his ancestors.
Performing the duties of a man,
he does not regret them later;
for day by day a person wastes away.
He who thinks, "I will do it tomorrow," neglects the task that ought to be done today;
he falls away from it thereafter.
Therefore, my dear, being heedful and free from anger, perform your duties;
exert yourself in your tasks.
The indolent man finds no happiness.
Even if he is of low birth,
the man who is industrious and resolute—
Endowed with conduct and virtue,
he shines like a fire, O Nigaṇṭha,
he who has performed what was to be done in the past.
Later he wishes to do it;
like one who has broken a varuṇa branch,
he later regrets it.
One who does not exert himself when it is time to exert,
though young and strong, yet given over to laziness,
with a mind of unwholesome intent and indolent—
The lazy person does not find the path through wisdom.
In this world, the foolish man is indolent and deficient in energy.
One who has heard little and behaves improperly falls away from growth.
This person, having heard little...
Like an ox, he merely grows old;
his flesh increases,
but his wisdom does not increase.
For that person who has become human,
yet possesses neither wealth nor craft—
what fruit is there in his humanity?
For that deer is indeed a two-legged beast who lives for a hundred years,
yet is indolent and lacking in energy.
A single day of life is better for one who exerts firm energy and knows the analysis of the Dhamma.
One who rises early and is untiring,
who applies themselves at the proper time,
finds that their fruit succeeds.
Having lived the holy life without having acquired wealth in youth,
they brood like aged curlews.
Like a fishless pond,
one who has not practiced the holy life and failed to acquire wealth in youth—
Like arrows shot from a bow,
they do not reach the old [teachings] by mere recitation;
for even with a little, the wise person—
The wise man, by means of what he has received, uplifts himself,
like a small fire that is being fanned.
A wise person should indeed exert effort and not become despondent;
behold the fruit of such exertion!
Having eaten mangoes that lack tradition,
that lack practice, and lack effort,
one attains happiness therein.
Go there, O Suvīra, and cause Mañca to go right there,
where one is indolent and fails to exert oneself.
One attains ultimate happiness;
go there with firm resolve,
and cause me to go there as well.
In this world, the fruit of one's intention is accomplished for the steadfast; therefore,
energy alone must be exerted.
This has been praised by the Buddhas.
[From] the Exposition of Wisdom (Paññā-niddesa): One should first seek wisdom.
The power of wisdom is most supreme;
for a son of noble family, wisdom is his strength—
what indeed cannot be accomplished by it?
The weapon that severs manifold doubts,
that reveals what is beyond the senses,
and that is the eye for all— this is the Teaching.
He for whom there is no blindness—
wisdom has cut through his learning,
increasing his fame and renown.
A person endowed with wisdom in this world finds happiness even [in difficult circumstances].
[This applies to] the Omniscient Buddhas and the Paccekabuddhas...
Regarding the phrase "those who have heard the Four Truths": among four Buddhas,
there would be only one man who is a man of great learning (bahussuta).
Skilled in writing, skilled in speech,
skilled in books, eloquent in recitation;
skilled in exposition and heroic—
Free from suffering, one performs one's own duties.
For the wise say that wisdom is supreme among wholesome qualities,
just as the king of stars is supreme among the constellations.
Virtue, glory, and the Dhamma of the good follow after the wisdom of the wise.
One should serve the Buddhas, those who are skillful and learned.
One who learns by heart, one who asks questions,
and one who listens attentively to well-spoken words—
a mortal acting in this way becomes wise.
By means of wind, by inquiries concerning fame,
by staying and dwelling with proper reflection,
through discussion, and through affectionate association.
And by means of suitable dwelling.
These eight factors are the causes for the clarification of the intellect.
For those in whom these arise, their wisdom blossoms.
(64) "Monks, there are these four things that lead to the growth of wisdom. What are the four? Association with superior persons..."
Hearing the true Dhamma, wise attention, and practice in accordance with the Dhamma— these, monks,
are the four things that lead to the increase of wisdom.
One endowed with the clarity of the eye...
One sees even that which is dazzlingly bright;
the blind man and the one-eyed man see clearly,
while the blind man sees nothing at all.
One who is walking sees one who is walking and one who is not walking;
one who is not walking sees one who is not walking.
And one does not see that which is passing away.
Visible form, which is manifest and uncovered, is seen by the physical eye.
With the eye of knowledge, one perceives everything exactly as it is—
neither more nor less— whether they be virtuous or non-virtuous beings.
Even those possessed of virtue do not associate with the secluded when they are in the presence of people who lack seclusion.
But he who does not quickly awaken to a matter that has arisen falls under the power of his enemies.
And afterwards one regrets it.
Thus wisdom is of great power,
subtle, and well-considering.
For the sake of welfare in this very life,
or for happiness in the future—
this is the best of strengths among strengths.
The foremost power is the power of wisdom;
supported by the power of wisdom,
the wise person finds success here.
The jewel of knowledge that has been obtained—
by which knowledge the Noble Ones awaken to the state of having accomplished their task.
Strive, O sons of the Conqueror! For one who wears the garland of the jewel of wisdom,
existence does not endure for long.
He quickly shows the Deathless,
yet he does not delight in existence; they, however,
devote themselves to negligence.
Foolish people are lacking in wisdom;
but the wise person guards heedfulness as if it were their most excellent wealth.
The wise man passes his time through the acquisition of wealth, merit, and wisdom;
the foolish man passes it through play.
When the wise man dispels sleep by means of wakefulness, or strife by means of harmony, or negligence by means of diligence;
Having ascended the palace of wisdom,
free from sorrow, he looks upon the sorrowing people like one standing on a mountain peak gazes down upon those on the ground.
The wise man observes the fool:
there is no love equal to oneself,
and there is no wealth equal to grain.
There is no radiance equal to wisdom;
rain is indeed supreme among floods.
And whatever benefit there is in this visible world—
One who understands the goal pertaining to the future,
through the realization of that goal,
is called wise and a sage.
One does not become wise merely by speaking much; rather,
it is one who dwells in security, free from enmity and fear.
He is called a wise man in whom truth, the Dhamma, non-violence,
self-restraint, and self-control reside.
He who has indeed cast off impurity is wise;
he is called an elder (thera).
[One should know] one's own virtues and one's own faults.
He who knows the virtues and the faults of others is wise;
he who knows this is wise.
He who practices the modes of conduct with mindfulness, energy,
and wisdom— verily, he shall be a wise man.
Grasping at both ends:
one who is grateful, endowed with knowledge,
of noble birth, and possessed of wealth.
Thus, one whose nature is reflective investigation shall become wise and free from suffering;
all beings are the owners of their own karma.
Kamma divides beings:
he who sees it as having the nature of direct experience,
and he who sees it as having the nature of saṃsāra among them.
The latter is to be honored because it is well-seen in both respects;
with little and blameless [effort].
Content with what is easily obtained,
knowing moderation and being easy to support,
a wise person should live their life.
First, one should establish oneself in what is appropriate;
only then should one instruct others.
The wise person should not be distressed.
Indeed, in the midst of the highest assembly,
the best speaker should utter the most excellent speech.
If one were to speak of it in brief or in detail,
it would be priceless throughout the three worlds—
the well-spoken words of the wise.
Only the wise person understands this;
the dull-witted do not know it,
but the steadfast cherish what is steadfast.
If by any means whatsoever another person receives satisfaction, and if there is purpose in one's speech,
[then that speech is well-spoken].
A wise person should not speak such things. One should not say,
"The mouth exists for the purpose of eating and for the purpose of speaking."
Whatever words a wise man utters from his mouth, whether they be beneficial to others or beneficial to himself,
[they are well-spoken].
For it is difficult for a man to know himself;
if he cannot even know his own strength,
what need is there to speak of the strength of others?
The wise person who repays a good deed done by others knows how to do so and explains it accordingly.
The fool does not appreciate virtue.
One should not do too much,
nor should one dwell on what will happen in the future.
The wise ones wander about according to the present time;
when there is mindfulness regarding phenomena, it is desired.
Salt is desired among flavors;
a minister for the king's duties;
and a wise man in all circumstances.
Among those who rely on their lineage, the khattiya is best;
but one endowed with true knowledge and conduct—
Thus he is the best among gods and humans.
The Fully Awakened One is the best of bipeds;
the thoroughbred is the best of quadrupeds.
Of wives, the obedient is best;
of sons, the one who listens;
and purposefulness with freedom from delusion.
Likewise, a suitable resort—
these four one should train in,
increasing clear comprehension.
No one attains wisdom without being obedient,
nor without approaching one who is learned.
The meaning established by the Dhamma is inseparable;
since the intended meaning exists within the Canon, it is very difficult to understand.
Therefore, one who knows what is heavy and what is weighty should take up the support. —
From the *Cāritta-niddesa* (Exposition on Conduct)
For oneself is indeed one's own protector;
for who else could be the protector?
By means of a self that is well-tamed, [one protects oneself].
One finds a Protector who is hard to find.
If one should know oneself to be dear,
one should protect it well-guarded.
During one of the three watches of the night,
the wise person should remain awake;
by this, he creates fortune for himself.
One makes oneself fortunate or unfortunate;
for no one else is the maker of another's fortune or misfortune.
The wise, though oppressed by their own suffering,
do not abandon actions that bear the fruit of happiness; nor do they,
even when deluded and intoxicated by pleasure, [abandon them].
They do not perform evil deeds.
He who takes up neither blame nor praise, neither censure nor honor;
Fortune and glory depart from him,
just as water flows away from dry land after a good rain; therefore,
it is well for a king to delight in the Dhamma.
Blessed is the man possessed of wisdom;
blessed is he who does not deceive his friends;
blessed is the doing of no evil.
The doer of good reaps good,
and the doer of evil reaps evil;
whatever kind of seed one sows, [that is what one harvests].
Such is the fruit one reaps.
One should protect one's life through wisdom;
one should protect one's wealth through industry.
"Thus indeed is one free from disease and happy"—
this is an ancient saying.
Gradually, the wise one...
Little by little, moment by moment,
as a smith refines silver,
one should cleanse away one's own impurities.
Guarding speech, well-restrained in mind,
and not performing unwholesome deeds with the body—
one should purify these three paths of action.
One should strive for the path proclaimed by the Seer.
A wise person should not associate with the wicked, but should associate with the virtuous.
The unwholesome go to hell;
the wholesome attain a happy destination. Even if one does not commit evil, [one is still affected by it].
He associates with one who is doing so;
he becomes suspected of evil,
and his ill-repute spreads.
Even a mango tree, though surrounded by undesirable things,
bears sweet fruit; whereas the *pā* tree,
though formerly bitter, remains bitter.
But that person who lives as a physician,
serving those who are base,
always sinks lower.
He shall never decline,
even when associating with those equal to himself;
endowed with beauty, fragrance, and flavor, he remains supreme.
Formerly you were an ambo tree;
while receiving that very same veneration,
why has the ambo tree now borne bitter fruit?
O Dadhivāhana, you have an *ambo* tree surrounded by *pucimanda* trees;
root is conjoined with root.
One should resort from branch to branch;
through living with those who are not harmonious,
that association bears bitter fruit.
One who desires their own welfare and prosperity should quickly associate with a superior person who is a leader.
One should associate even more so with such a person by means of oneself.
Therefore the wise man rises up.
Just as glass, through contact with gold,
assumes the brilliance of a gem.
Likewise, through close association,
even a fool attains proficiency; even a worm,
through contact with a *sumana* flower, [becomes fragrant].
He ascends to the head of the virtuous;
through this, he even attains divinity,
well-established upon the great waters.
One should dwell only with the virtuous,
one should associate with the virtuous;
having understood the true Dhamma of the good.
One gains wisdom from no one else.
One should associate only with the virtuous;
one should cultivate intimacy only with the virtuous.
Having understood the true Dhamma,
one is liberated from all suffering; indeed,
O son of noble family, [one does so] only once.
There is meeting with the virtuous;
that association protects one,
not frequenting those who are not virtuous.
Better is a wise friend who has compassion for fools,
than one who is virtuous and wise [but lacks such compassion].
Seeking one who provides dependence during the day, and who is learned,
one who prizes his own welfare should associate with such a person.
Having avoided evil friends,
one should associate with the supreme person;
and one should abide by his instruction.
Aspiring for unshakable happiness,
one should not associate with evil friends,
nor should one associate with the lowest of men.
One should associate with virtuous friends;
one should associate with the most excellent of men.
Their speech is blameless and their countenance is pure.
The speech of a man is like the Bharata epic:
it shines when adorned;
how could it be beautiful without its adornments?
For even one endowed with beauty,
sweet-voiced and pleasant to look upon,
does not become beloved if their speech is harsh.
In this world and in the next,
do we not see this Kālī,
so ill-favored and covered with moles?
One who is gentle in speech is dear to many living beings;
therefore, one should speak with kindly words.
Speaking with wisdom and free from agitation,
he illuminates both the meaning and the Dhamma;
his speech is sweet.
One should speak only that speech which does not cause distress to living beings and does not harm others.
That indeed is well-spoken speech;
one should speak only pleasant words,
those words that are welcomed with joy.
That which, without taking up evil deeds,
one speaks as something pleasing to others—
truth indeed is the deathless word.
This is the eternal Dhamma;
in truth, in the goal, and in the Dhamma,
the virtuous are said to be firmly established.
Well-spoken words, the Dhamma,
what is pleasing, and truth itself—
endowed with these four factors, [it is a gift].
A wise person should speak words;
they should speak only what is pleasing,
never what is displeasing.
For one who speaks agreeably,
even a simple remedy becomes effective;
whatever he says, that shall be done.
What one does not say, that one does not do; the wise clearly recognize one who speaks without acting.
One should not speak behind someone's back,
nor should one speak of their faults in their presence;
one should speak without haste.
Do not speak harshly; do not say anything cruel,
for those who are addressed may retort against you.
For contentious speech is painful;
retaliation may strike you back.
Perform only such action as is appropriate for yourself.
Speak words that are appropriate;
wealth is lost through what is inappropriate,
and life perishes through what is inappropriate.
Those people who honor the aged,
being well-versed in the Dhamma,
are praised even in this present life.
And in the life hereafter, a happy destination.
One should speak words that are refined,
for speech that is well-composed is truly excellent.
A mere brother is called "brother," and a mere father is called "father.
So too are giving and speaking kindly.
And the eightfold conduct found here,
as well as impartiality toward all things,
each according to what is appropriate in each case.
Kings speak but once;
ascetics and brahmins speak but once;
so too do men in the world speak but once.
This is the eternal law:
one who is compassionate may speak either one word or two words.
One should not speak further in the presence of a slave-merchant; by doing so,
one becomes even worse off than he.
He who returns anger for anger—
by not returning anger for one who is angry,
he conquers a battle difficult to win.
He acts for the benefit of both himself and another,
having recognized that the other is provoked to anger.
He who, being mindful, attains tranquility—
protecting himself, he protects others;
protecting others, he protects himself.
Patience is the cause for virtue, concentration, and wisdom;
indeed, all wholesome states [arise from it].
They indeed prosper by depending on forbearance;
what can a wicked person do against one who wields the sword of patience?
Fire that has fallen upon dry grass extinguishes itself; likewise,
through obedience and listening, [wisdom grows].
Grasping and likewise retaining,
as well as consciousness for the purpose of reasoning and reflection, and the knowledge of reality— these are the qualities of wisdom.
In whomsoever among people these four qualities exist, he is wise:
truthfulness, righteousness, fortitude, and generosity.
He transcends what is seen:
the physician, the chaplain, the counselor,
and the fourth, the one who knows the Vedas.
One who desires constant personal glory should visit friends at the break of dawn.
If, at the proper time, one has gathered much wealth that might otherwise perish,
one should distribute it among friends.
One should not look at the faults of others,
nor at what they have done or left undone; one should examine only oneself.
Whether deeds have been done or left undone,
people follow after them according to their country, birth, and former conduct.
Knowing that the illusion which pierces others is actually a friend, one should mount the raft of protection made of wood.
Just as one might sink in the great ocean,
so too does even a person of virtuous life sink by associating with one who is indolent.
Therefore, one should avoid that person who is lazy and deficient in energy;
for laziness and negligence [lead to ruin].
Lack of exertion and lack of restraint,
as well as sleep and sloth— these are the openings;
one should avoid them entirely.
One should shun the wicked fool as a young man would a venomous snake;
one should break apart evil karma.
Like an elephant in a reed-hut,
for there is no union between those whose minds are different—
neither between women nor between men.
Avoiding association with various kinds of people,
one should not even associate with such as these;
one should not associate with those who have committed evil.
We do not trust the speaker of falsehood;
we do not trust one whose wisdom is directed toward his own self-interest,
nor do we trust one who is himself at peace.
The elephant-posture, the black snake,
the head-anointed king, and all women—
a man who is always mindful should avoid these.
Indeed, the true nature of both women and the wicked is difficult to discern;
trust in them should never be placed.
In Viśeṣa, Siṅgi, Nadi, Roga, and Rājakula;
the woman-debauchee, the liquor-debauchee—
And that man who is a gambler at dice,
who squanders whatever he gains—
that is a cause of his downfall.
Having evil friends, evil companions,
and evil conduct as one's sphere of activity,
[one falls] from this world and the next.
A person falls away from both:
fame is destroyed by stinginess,
and virtue is destroyed by anger.
Truth is lost through deceit;
the protection of the Dhamma through meanness;
and wealth through the goddess of dice.
There is destruction and calamity;
stability is destroyed and there is negligence;
the twice-born and the bhikkhu perish.
By backbiting a family is ruined;
by pride, oneself is ruined;
by misconduct, a human being [is ruined].
The heir of poverty is destroyed;
where there is disrespect, there is even the disparagement of one's own peace.
One should not dwell in a place where there is contempt for the lowly; rather,
one should live where both the lazy and the skillful are honored.
Both the brave and the cowardly may be honored there,
but the virtuous do not dwell among men who make no distinction between them.
If he possesses neither his own wisdom nor is well-trained in the Vinaya,
he is like a blind buffalo in the forest.
Many people would practice [this].
Indeed, the fruit destroys the plantain tree;
the fruit destroys the bamboo, the fruit destroys the reed.
Honors kill a man, just as a fetus kills a mule;
having recognized a fault as a fault, [one should avoid it].
And what is blameless as blameless;
through the undertaking of right view,
beings go to a happy destination.
The Exposition on Household Life:
It is better to live as a householder,
sharing food with others, than to live as a monk while being stingy.
Laughter amidst the pursuit of gain,
and lack of distress when one's purpose fails;
he who here [endures] both cold and heat—
He does not think more highly of himself than a blade of grass;
performing his human duties,
he is not separated from happiness.
Wise, endowed with virtue,
gentle and eloquent,
living in a sheltered manner and free from arrogance.
Such a person gains renown:
industrious and not lazy,
he does not tremble in times of misfortune.
The wise one of unbroken conduct,
such as he, gains renown;
he is a gatherer and a maker of friends.
Generous, free from stinginess,
a leader, a guide, and one who follows the right path—
such a person gains renown.
For one who is diligent, mindful,
pure in action, acting with circumspection,
self-restrained, and living according to the Dhamma—
The fame of one who is heedful increases.
There are, dear son, only two footprints by which everything is established: [the footprint of virtue and the footprint of wisdom].
The gaining of what has not been gained,
and the preservation of what has been gained—
one should divide one's wealth into four parts.

Having plunged into the Piṭakas,

Let those who seek this essence,

Naradakkha’s Praise and Benediction 2.
Verse:
He who was born here as Pālitodha,
He is indeed a venerable elder,
truly marvelous; he is Mahāpālita the holy one,
and he is Nikāyapālita.
May they see this book of human skill,
which bestows human skill upon those with little leisure;
may people see it rightly.
May they attain the state of a donor.
